methods.label: Find the corner-triangle legs
methods.explanation:
The side lengths of the inner and outer squares are \(20/4=5\) and \(28/4=7\). With one inner vertex on each outer side, the gaps at the four outer corners are right triangles whose hypotenuses are the inner square's sides.

These triangles are congruent: their hypotenuses all have length \(5\), and their acute angles match because consecutive sides of each square are perpendicular. Let their two leg lengths be \(u\ge v>0\). Each outer side is divided into segments of lengths \(u\) and \(v\), so
\[
u+v=7.
\]
The Pythagorean theorem gives \(u^2+v^2=25\). These two relations reveal the difference of the legs:
\[
(u-v)^2=2(u^2+v^2)-(u+v)^2
=50-49=1.
\]
Since \(u\ge v\), we have \(u-v=1\). Together with \(u+v=7\), this gives \(u=4\) and \(v=3\).

Every inner vertex therefore divides its outer side into lengths \(3\) and \(4\). Its distances to the endpoints of that side are \(3\) and \(4\). Its distances to the other two outer vertices are, by the Pythagorean theorem,
\[
\sqrt{7^2+3^2}=\sqrt{58}
\quad\text{and}\quad
\sqrt{7^2+4^2}=\sqrt{65}.
\]
These four possibilities account for every inner-to-outer vertex pair. The greatest distance is \(\boxed{\sqrt{65}}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
